spans.assertion: the analysis used data on 146,028 player-referee dyads from four major European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain) in the 2012-2013 season to examine whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players

the primary estimand, the adjusted risk difference, was 0.178 percentage points (95% CI -0.003 to 0.360, p=0.054), indicating dark-skinned players have a marginally higher probability of receiving a red card
the secondary estimand, the adjusted odds ratio, was 1.158 (95% CI 0.997 to 1.344, p=0.054)
the hypothesis is concluded NOT SUPPORTED because the 95% CI barely crosses zero and p=0.054 exceeds the α=0.05 threshold, making the evidence inconclusive
sensitivity analyses using alternative specifications (continuous skin tone, full sample) yielded statistically significant results (p<0.05)
the effect size is small but consistently positive across all specifications
the adjusted risk difference point estimate was 0.178 percentage points (0.001784), with a 95% CI of -0.003 to 0.360 percentage points
a two-sided significance test with α=0.05 was used for the risk difference
the p-value for the adjusted risk difference was 0.0544
the risk difference estimate was adjusted for exposure (games played), player characteristics, position, and league
the confidence interval for the risk difference barely includes zero, making the result marginally non-significant
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.158 with a 95% CI of 0.997 to 1.344
the p-value for the adjusted odds ratio was 0.0544
dark-skinned players have 15.8% higher odds of receiving a red card than light-skinned players, adjusting for covariates
the confidence interval for the odds ratio barely includes 1.0 (no effect)

spans.note: section break into Model and Estimation Details

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad, with N=115,603 after exclusions
the mean number of dyads per player was 81.5 and per referee was 39.8
the analysis sample comprised 115,603 total dyads, 1,419 unique players, 2,904 unique referees, and 350,448 total games
1,455 dyads (1.26%) had at least one red card; 89,107 dyads (77.1%) involved light-skinned players and 26,496 dyads (22.9%) involved dark-skinned players
the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of any red card received (1) versus none (0) in the dyad
red cards are rare events, occurring in only 1.26% of dyads

spans.note: Exposure Variable / Skin Tone Categorization subheading

spans.assertion: skin tone was independently rated by two blind raters on a 5-point scale from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
the inter-rater correlation for skin tone ratings was 0.923, indicating excellent agreement
the two raters' skin tone scores were averaged into a single skin_tone_avg variable
the averaged skin tone score was dichotomized into light (<0.5) versus dark (≥0.5)
the crude (unadjusted) red card rate was 1.23% for light-skinned players and 1.35% for dark-skinned players, a crude risk difference of 0.12 percentage points
the model adjusted for log(games played), standardized player age, standardized height, standardized weight, position (12 categories), and league country (4 categories)
21,407 dyads were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings (no player photo available)
9,018 dyads were excluded due to missing covariates (position, height, weight)
the final analysis sample was 115,603 dyads out of the original 146,028
a logistic regression was used to predict the binary outcome of any red card
standard errors were clustered at the player level to account for correlation among multiple dyads per player
average marginal effects were calculated to obtain risk differences on the probability scale
the model was estimated using maximum likelihood estimation with statsmodels in Python
the fitted model formula was any_red_card ~ skin_dark + log_games + age_std + height_std + weight_std + C(position) + C(leagueCountry)
the model's estimated coefficients were: skin_dark OR=1.158 (p=0.054), log_games OR=2.669 (p<0.001), age_std OR=1.008 (p=0.823), height_std OR=0.954 (p=0.461), weight_std OR=1.078 (p=0.181)
the number of games played was the strongest predictor of red cards (OR=2.67 per log-unit increase)
player age, height, and weight showed no significant association with red cards
position and league country showed significant associations with red cards
five alternative model specifications were run to assess robustness of the findings
the primary full-adjustment model (N=115,603) found a risk difference of 0.178pp (95% CI -0.003 to 0.360), p=0.054
an extremes-only model (skin tone 0 vs 1, N=38,359) found a risk difference of 0.270pp (95% CI -0.055 to 0.594), p=0.107
a model using continuous skin tone (N=115,603) found a risk difference of 0.290pp (95% CI 0.019 to 0.561), p=0.037
a minimal model with only games as a covariate (N=115,603) found a risk difference of 0.171pp (95% CI -0.009 to 0.350), p=0.062
a full-sample model with only games as a covariate (N=124,621) found a risk difference of 0.177pp (95% CI 0.006 to 0.348), p=0.043
effect estimates were remarkably consistent (0.17-0.29pp) across the five specifications
the continuous skin tone model and the full sample model achieved p<0.05
results were not sensitive to covariate adjustment, as the minimal and full models were nearly identical
the extremes-only analysis showed the largest effect but a wider confidence interval due to smaller sample size
the hypothesis is concluded NOT SUPPORTED at α=0.05 based on the primary estimand, since the CI barely includes zero and p=0.054 marginally exceeds the threshold
the evidence, while not statistically significant, is characterized as borderline and trending in the hypothesized direction
the point estimate consistently suggests a small positive association (0.18pp)
alternative specifications yielded p-values below 0.05 (continuous: p=0.037; full sample: p=0.043)
all sensitivity analyses showed positive effects in the same direction
the confidence interval is described as very close to excluding zero
the adjusted risk difference of 0.18pp represents a 14.5% relative increase over the baseline red card rate for light-skinned players (1.23%)
it is suggested this marginal effect could represent a meaningful disparity at the population level given the large number of games played
in absolute terms the effect corresponds to approximately 1.8 additional red cards per 1,000 dyads for dark-skinned players
it is suggested cumulative effects over seasons and leagues could represent systemic bias worthy of attention

spans.note: section break into Limitations, Measurement Issues subheading

spans.assertion: skin tone classification was based on static profile photos rather than live in-game assessment
the choice of 0.5 as the dichotomization threshold is acknowledged as somewhat arbitrary
the red card outcome was aggregated over the entire dyad history rather than measured per individual game
the analysis did not distinguish between direct red cards and second yellow cards
country-level implicit/explicit referee bias measures existed in the data but were not used in the model

spans.note: caveat about unavailable game context variables

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players are distributed differently across playing positions than light-skinned players, and defensive positions may draw more cards
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing player photos, which could bias results if the missingness is non-random
9,018 additional dyads were excluded due to missing covariates
a sensitivity analysis using the full sample showed results similar to the main analysis despite this exclusion
the sample was limited to male players from four European leagues, which may limit generalizability to other contexts
no adjustment for multiple testing was made across the sensitivity analyses
standard errors were clustered by player
two-way clustering by player and referee was not used, which may underestimate uncertainty
the exposure modeling assumes a linear relationship between log(games) and the logit scale, which may not perfectly capture exposure
the study used an observational design, which cannot establish causality
the analysis could not distinguish implicit bias from differential treatment due to correlated behaviors
the linearity-of-log-odds assumption was reasonably satisfied given the log-transformation of games
no perfect multicollinearity was found among predictors
independence after clustering was assumed, though this assumption was not fully testable
the average marginal effects approach assumes the effect is constant across the covariate distribution

spans.note: section break into Methodological Transparency, Variable Transformations subheading

spans.assertion: skin tone ratings were averaged across the two raters
the averaged skin tone score was dichotomized at a threshold of 0.5
games played was transformed using a natural log to address its right-skewed distribution
continuous covariates were standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 for better convergence
missing data were handled via complete-case analysis with listwise deletion
a full-sample sensitivity analysis (N=124,621) with minimal covariates showed consistent results
standard errors were clustered by player ID to account for within-player correlation across dyads
the clustering approach was conservative, producing larger standard errors than naive standard errors
the analysis was conducted in Python 3.11 using pandas, numpy, statsmodels, and scikit-learn
the full reproducible code was provided in final_analysis.py
no bootstrapping or simulation was used, so no random seed was required

spans.note: section break into Additional Findings, Covariates subheading

spans.assertion: games played was the strongest predictor of red cards, with more exposure associated with more red cards
center backs had the highest red card rates and wingers the lowest, relative to attacking midfielders
Spain and France had higher red card rates than England and Germany
age, height, and weight showed no significant associations with red cards

spans.note: Distribution Differences by Skin Tone subheading

spans.assertion: dark-skinned players were more concentrated in forward positions (20% vs 13% for light-skinned players)
dark-skinned players were more common in England (37% vs 24%) and France (26% vs 11%)
dark-skinned players were less common in Germany (20% vs 37%) and Spain (17% vs 28%)
dark-skinned players were slightly younger (26.9 vs 27.3 years) and shorter (181.6 vs 182.3cm)
these distributional differences between dark- and light-skinned players are said to underscore the importance of covariate adjustment
the analysis is characterized as providing suggestive but inconclusive evidence, with the primary estimand narrowly missing statistical significance
all models showed positive effects (0.17-0.29pp), described as consistency
some alternative specifications achieved p<0.05
the direction of effects unambiguously favors the hypothesis
at the conventional α=0.05 threshold, the conclusion is that the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
the evidence is characterized as borderline and warranting further investigation with larger samples, more detailed behavioral data, or experimental designs to establish causality

it is suggested that small systematic biases could accumulate to meaningful disparities over time, and the consistent positive associations warrant attention from soccer governing bodies despite not reaching conventional significance
